submitLabel: Your platform audit, the records decision, and the write-up
intro: Paste the platform audit including what is on by default, the consent map flagged for counsel, the written records decision with your actual consent sentence, the counsel questions, your predicted count of transcription-capable platforms scored against what you found, and the 300–400 word write-up. No case facts — this activity produces a process decision. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext: You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Labor & Employee Relations track — for ER specialists and investigators, ER centres of excellence, labor relations managers and contract administrators who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 3 applied activity, 'The records decision'. OVERRIDING FIRST CHECK: no case facts. This activity produces a process decision; if the submission describes a real interview, witness, or matter, flag it at the top, request resubmission with it removed, and do not grade substance. The activity has five parts. (1) A platform audit: every platform an investigation interview could happen on — video conferencing, telephony, room systems, collaboration tools — and for each, whether transcription or an AI notetaker is available and whether it is ON BY DEFAULT, whether a participant can see it running, and whether the investigator can turn it off in the moment, plus what they could not determine and who owns that answer. (2) A consent map: which jurisdictions their investigations reach, which require all-party consent as far as they know — FLAGGED FOR COUNSEL RATHER THAN ASSERTED — and what current practice actually is when a participant is in one. (3) The written decision for their Module 1 matter type: what is captured at which stage by what tool including explicitly what happens at first contact; the consent language written as the sentence they would actually say; who reviews machine output against contemporaneous notes before filing and what they check, including attribution, unmarked inaudibility, and quality BY SPEAKER; retention; and the one thing they have decided NOT to record and why. (4) Two or three counsel questions naming the platform and jurisdictions. (5) The prediction scored. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS: a defensible 'we don't record' is a FULL-CREDIT answer to this entire activity — the graded thing is the reasoning, never the direction. Do not push learners toward recording. The module's core discipline is that a machine transcript is an aid to notes rather than a substitute: keep contemporaneous notes separately, review before filing, never file an unreviewed transcript, and make corrections visible and dated rather than silent. Reward the three mitigations: disclosing before rather than during, offering the alternative and meaning it, and never transcribing first contact. Reward checking transcription quality BY SPEAKER rather than in aggregate, since an overall accuracy figure hides exactly the pattern that matters — and reward a learner who concluded that for a particular speaker the answer is notes plus human review rather than a better tool. On consent, reward flagging for counsel over asserting a legal conclusion; the learner is not being graded on legal accuracy but on whether they produced something counsel could act on. Reward recognizing that the controlling question is where the PARTICIPANTS are rather than where the investigator is. Reward getting Weingarten right — it does not forbid recording, and the real constraints are consent law, candour, the collective agreement, and possibly the duty to bargain. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that the tool which improves your record degrades the investigation the record is of. Its real counter-argument is that this treats candour as fragile on thin evidence while flattering what notes actually are: notes are a selective reconstruction by an interested party and are attacked on exactly those grounds, a transcript defeats both 'that's not what I said' and 'the note omits my explanation', and it protects the people with least power — a complainant whose account was summarized by someone who found it implausible, and a respondent whose explanation was compressed. Also that the chilling argument proves too much, since people give evidence on the record in depositions and tribunals constantly, so the claim is about HR's informality rather than human psychology. THE WRITE-UP MUST ANSWER WHO BEARS THE COST under their chosen position — chilling costs the complainant who may not come forward, inaccurate notes cost the respondent whose explanation gets compressed — because deciding between them is deciding which party absorbs the risk of the process. A position that presents either option as simply better practice without naming who pays has not engaged the argument. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap.

opening.label: Predicted — platforms your investigations could use that have transcription available
opening.hint: Video, telephony, room systems, collaboration tools. Count before you look.

calibration.label: Actual — how many, and how many were on by default
calibration.hint: Give the total you found. Note the default-on count in your write-up.

dimensions.name: The platform audit found the defaults
dimensions.criteria: Every platform an interview could happen on, with the three operational questions answered: is transcription available, is it on by default, and can the investigator turn it off in the moment. The graded finding is a default-on capability the learner did not know about — that is the module's premise and discovering one should score at the top. Credit noting whether a participant can see it running. Credit naming what could not be determined and who owns that answer over guessing. An audit listing only the primary conferencing tool has missed telephony and room systems.

dimensions.name: The consent map is flagged, not asserted
dimensions.criteria: Jurisdictions the investigations reach, which are believed to require all-party consent, and what current practice is when a participant is in one. The graded behaviour is flagging for counsel rather than stating a legal conclusion — the learner is not being assessed on legal accuracy. Credit recognizing that the controlling question is where the PARTICIPANTS are rather than where the investigator is, since that is the operative point and the one most often reversed. Credit an honest statement that current practice is inconsistent or unknown.

dimensions.name: The decision is written, including what is not recorded
dimensions.criteria: A decision rather than a description of options: what is captured, at which stage, by what tool, with first contact addressed explicitly. The consent language must be written as the actual sentence the learner would say at the top of an interview — a policy paraphrase does not satisfy this. And the one thing they have decided not to record, with reasoning. A defensible 'we do not record at all' is full credit; the direction is never graded, only the reasoning. Credit the three mitigations where present: disclose before rather than during, offer the alternative, never transcribe first contact.

dimensions.name: Review before filing is specified, and checks by speaker
dimensions.criteria: A named person or role who reviews machine output against contemporaneous notes before it enters a file, and what they check. Three elements are graded: speaker attribution, unmarked inaudibility rendered as confident text, and **quality by speaker rather than in aggregate** — an overall accuracy figure hides exactly the pattern the disparity exposure is about. Top marks for a learner who concluded that where one participant's transcript is materially poorer the answer is notes plus human review, and that the call itself gets recorded. Credit specifying that corrections are visible and dated rather than silent.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: Predicted transcription-capable platforms against actual, plus the default-on count, with an account of the gap — an undercount is the intended finding and a discovered default-on capability is the best version of it. Accuracy is never graded. Plus a committed position on the module's claim engaging the real counter-argument: that notes are a selective reconstruction attacked on exactly those grounds, that a transcript defeats the two commonest challenges and protects the people with least power, and that the chilling argument proves too much given how routinely people give evidence on the record. THE POSITION MUST NAME WHO BEARS THE COST — chilling costs the complainant, compressed notes cost the respondent — because the choice allocates the risk of the process to one party or the other. A position presenting either option as simply better practice without naming who pays has not engaged the argument and should be told so.
